subject: Interpretation of parameter estimates from an EIRM model with only fixed effects

messages.author: 73b47663eb1c2067
messages.subject: Interpretation of parameter estimates from an EIRM model with only fixed effects
parts:
All,

Here are some results from an "explanatory item response model" that I fit with fixed effects for a number of person covariates (and a random effect for schools). The measurement model had one factor with 3 indicators. Is it correct to interpret the estimate for students in grade 10 as being more likely to endorse the items on the scale as compared to those in grade 8 (the reference)? Similarly, for outcome expectancies of smoking, is it correct to say that participants who thought that smoking would lead to more positive outcomes were more likely to endorse items on the scale than those who did not?

Is the idea in explanatory item response models that a scale/set of items under question is capturing/measuring some aspects of the covariates with statistically significant fixed effects after accounting for latent traits? How are these covariates "explaining" test-taking behavior on the scale? That's where I'm confused. I can't entirely figure out the substantive meaning of these parameters and so can't figure out if these models are getting at what I need, and the substantive literature on EIRM isn't very useful either.

I'm being vague on person because of some of the data disclosure issues with this particular study.

Thanks,


Sabeeh

On Mon, May 22, 2017 at 6:51 PM, Sabeeh Baig <sabeeh...@gmail.com> wrote:
All,

Here are some results from an "explanatory item response model" that I fit with fixed effects for a number of person covariates (and a random effect for schools). The measurement model had one factor with 3 indicators. Is it correct to interpret the estimate for students in grade 10 as being more likely to endorse the items on the scale as compared to those in grade 8 (the reference)?
Possibly. Though you should probably do a Wald test to confirm whether this is a statistically accurate statement.

Similarly, for outcome expectancies of smoking, is it correct to say that participants who thought that smoking would lead to more positive outcomes were more likely to endorse items on the scale than those who did not?

Is the idea in explanatory item response models that a scale/set of items under question is capturing/measuring some aspects of the covariates with statistically significant fixed effects after accounting for latent traits?
How are these covariates "explaining" test-taking behavior on the scale? That's where I'm confused.

It's the same way that regression analysis explains variability in the DV; in this case, the DV is the categorical responses. It might be helpful to see the associated paper with the mixedmirt() function, which is in in the reference section of the helpfile.

I can't entirely figure out the substantive meaning of these parameters and so can't figure out if these models are getting at what I need, and the substantive literature on EIRM isn't very useful either.

I'm being vague on person because of some of the data disclosure issues with this particular study.

Thanks,


Sabeeh
